questions.question: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?
questions.explanation:
Checking each grammar for ambiguity (does some string have two distinct parse trees?):

- [latex]S\rightarrow aSb\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates only [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], with a unique nested derivation for every string — unambiguous.
- [latex]E\rightarrow E+E\mid E*E\mid id[/latex]: the classic textbook example of an ambiguous grammar — e.g. [latex]id+id*id[/latex] can be parsed with two different groupings (no precedence/associativity is encoded), giving two distinct parse trees.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid Sa\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates strings of [latex]a[/latex]'s only, but because both left-recursion ([latex]Sa[/latex]) and right-recursion ([latex]aS[/latex]) are available, a string like "[latex]aa[/latex]" can be built in more than one structurally distinct way — ambiguous.
- [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid\epsilon[/latex]: purely right-recursive, unique derivation for every string — unambiguous.

Answer: [latex]E\rightarrow E+E|E*E|id[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow aS|Sa|\epsilon[/latex] are ambiguous.

questions.question: Which languages necessarily need heap allocation in the runtime environment?

options.C: Those that allow dynamic data structures

questions.explanation:
Recursion needs only a stack, and globals need only static memory. Dynamic data structures (linked lists, trees created at run time with malloc/new) need memory whose lifetime is not tied to calls, i.e. a heap.

Answer: Those that allow dynamic data structures

options.B: Symbol table is accessed only during the lexical analysis phase.
options.C: Data flow analysis is necessary for run-time memory management.

- Every deterministic CFL has an LR(1) grammar, so LR(1) parsing is sufficient for DCFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: LR(1) parsing is sufficient for deterministic context-free languages

questions.question:
Given the following syntax-directed translation rules:

[latex] \text{Rule 1: } R \rightarrow AB \{ B.i = R.i - 1; A.i = B.i; R.i = A.i + 1; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 2: } P \rightarrow CD \{ P.i = C.i + D.i; D.i = C.i + 2; \} [/latex]
[latex] \text{Rule 3: } Q \rightarrow EF \{ Q.i = E.i + F.i; \} [/latex]

Which ONE is the CORRECT option among the following?

options.A: Rule 1 is S-attributed and L-attributed;  Rule 2 is S-attributed and not L-attributed;  Rule 3 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.
options.B: Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is S-attributed and L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
options.C: Rule 1 is neither S-attributed nor L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.
options.D: Rule 1 is S-attributed and not L-attributed;  Rule 2 is not S-attributed and is L-attributed;  Rule 3 is S-attributed and L-attributed.

questions.explanation:
Classify each rule by whether it uses only synthesized attributes (S-attributed: every attribute is computed purely from children) versus whether it's L-attributed (inherited attributes may only depend on the parent or strictly-left siblings, evaluated left to right):

Rule 1 ([latex]R\to AB\{B.i=R.i-1;\ A.i=B.i;\ R.i=A.i+1;\}[/latex]): [latex]A.i[/latex] is defined using [latex]B.i[/latex] — but [latex]B[/latex] is to the right of [latex]A[/latex] in the production, so this inherited-attribute dependency flows backward (right-to-left), violating L-attributed rules. It's also not S-attributed, since [latex]B.i[/latex] is set from [latex]R.i[/latex] (an inherited attribute from the parent). Neither S-attributed nor L-attributed.

Rule 2 ([latex]P\to CD\{P.i=C.i+D.i;\ D.i=C.i+2;\}[/latex]): [latex]D.i[/latex] (inherited) is set using only [latex]C.i[/latex], a left sibling — perfectly valid for L-attributed. But since [latex]D[/latex] does have an inherited attribute at all, the SDT is not purely synthesized. Not S-attributed, but is L-attributed.

Rule 3 ([latex]Q\to EF\{Q.i=E.i+F.i;\}[/latex]): the only attribute defined is [latex]Q.i[/latex], computed purely from its children [latex]E,F[/latex] — purely synthesized. S-attributed (and therefore also L-attributed, since S-attributed is a special case of L-attributed).

Answer: Rule 1 is neither; Rule 2 is not S-attributed but is L-attributed; Rule 3 is both S-attributed and L-attributed.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding the front-end and back-end of a compiler.

S1: The front-end includes phases that are independent of the target hardware.
S2: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the target hardware.
S3: The back-end includes phases that are specific to the programming language used in the source code.

Identify the CORRECT option.

options.B: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE.
options.C: S1, S2, and S3 are all TRUE.
options.D: Only S1 and S3 are TRUE.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Front end (lexical, syntax, semantic analysis, intermediate code) depends on the source language, not on the target machine [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S1 TRUE.
- Back end (code optimization for the machine, code generation) is specific to the target hardware [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S2 TRUE.
- The back end works on intermediate code, so it is independent of the source language [latex]\text{---}[/latex] S3 FALSE.

Answer: Only S1 and S2 are TRUE

questions.question:
Consider the following two sets of LR(1) items of an LR(1) grammar.

[latex]\begin{array}{l|l} X \rightarrow c.X, c∕d &X → c.X, \$\\ X \rightarrow .cX, c∕  d& X → .cX, \$\\ X \rightarrow .d, c∕ d & X → .d, \$ \end{array}[/latex]

Which of the following statements related to merging of the two sets in the corresponding LALR parser is/are FALSE?
1. Cannot be merged since look aheads are different.
2. Can be merged but will result in S-R conflict.
3. Can be merged but will result in R-R conflict.
4. Cannot be merged since goto on c will lead to two different sets.
questions.explanation:
Both sets have the same core (same items, different lookaheads), so LALR merges them. The merged set has no reduce items (only shifts on c and d), so there is no S-R or R-R conflict. GOTO on c from both lead to sets that are also merged.

So all four statements are false.

Answer: 1, 2, 3 and 4

questions.question:
For a statement S in a program, in the context of liveness analysis, the following sets are defined:

USE(S) : the set of variables used in S
IN(S) : the set of variables that are live at the entry of S
OUT(S) : the set of variables that are live at the exit of S

Consider a basic block that consists of two statements, S1 followed by S2. Which one of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation:

questions.question:
Consider the productions [latex]A\rightarrow PQ[/latex] and [latex]A\rightarrow XY[/latex]. Each of the five non-terminals A,P,Q,X, and Y has two attributes: s is a synthesized attribute, and i is an inherited attribute. Consider the following rules.

Rule 1: P.i=A.i+2, Q.i=P.i+A.i, and A.s=P.s+Q.s
Rule 2: X.i=A.i+Y.s and Y.i=X.s+A.i

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: Both Rule 1 and Rule 2 are L-attributed.
options.D: Neither Rule 1 nor Rule 2 is L-attributed.

questions.explanation:
L-attributed: an inherited attribute may depend only on the parent's inherited attributes and on attributes of siblings to its left.

- Rule 1: P.i uses A.i; Q.i uses P.i (left sibling) and A.i [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] L-attributed.
- Rule 2: X.i uses Y.s, and Y is to the right of X [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not L-attributed.

Answer: Only Rule 1 is L-attributed
